mcq.q: What happens to baseline physiological performance capacities (e.g., VO2max, muscle strength, submaximal cardiac output) across different phases of the menstrual cycle?

mcq.q: Which formula correctly defines Energy Availability (EA) in exercise physiology?

EA = Fat Mass / Caloric Intake
mcq.rationale: Energy Availability is defined as dietary energy intake (EI) minus exercise energy expenditure (EEE), normalized to fat-free mass (FFM in kg): EA = (EI - EEE) / FFM.

mcq.q: What is the clinical term for abnormally infrequent or irregular menstruation characterized by cycle lengths exceeding 35 days (fewer than 9 cycles/year)?

Oligomenorrhea

Suppression of active thyroid hormone (T3), leptin, and IGF-1

sa.prompt: Define secondary amenorrhea, state the mathematical formula for Energy Availability (EA), and detail the neuroendocrine mechanisms by which low energy availability causes menstrual disruption.
sa.model: Secondary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menstruation for 90 days or longer in a previously eumenorrheic female. Energy Availability is calculated as EA = (Energy Intake - Exercise Energy Expenditure) / Fat-Free Mass (kg). When an athlete experiences chronic low energy availability (<30 kcal/kg FFM/day), the severe caloric deficit suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility, which disrupts anterior pituitary LH pulse frequency and amplitude. Disrupted LH pulsatility impairs ovarian follicular development, causing severe hypoestrogenemia (low circulating estrogen) and progesterone deficiency. Additionally, low EA triggers a starvation response, suppressing active thyroid hormone (T3), leptin, and IGF-1.
criteria: Define secondary amenorrhea (absence of menses for >=90 days in previously eumenorrheic female).
State the EA formula: EA = (EI - EEE) / FFM (kg).
Detail neuroendocrine disruption: low EA (<30 kcal/kg FFM/day) alters GnRH/LH pulsatility, causing hypoestrogenemia and suppressing T3/leptin.

sa.prompt: Explain textbook evidence regarding athletic performance stability across the phases of the normal menstrual cycle, and contrast energy deficit versus exercise stress as causes of amenorrhea.
sa.model: Textbook evidence demonstrates that baseline physiological capacities—including VO2max, submaximal cardiorespiratory kinetics, muscle strength, anaerobic power, and lactate threshold—remain fully preserved and stable across the early follicular, late follicular, and luteal phases of the menstrual cycle, with no systemic performance decline. World records and Olympic gold medals have been achieved across all cycle phases. Regarding causation, landmark experiments prove that exercise stress per se does not cause amenorrhea; when caloric intake is expanded to match high exercise energy expenditure (maintaining EA >= 45 kcal/kg FFM/day), LH pulsatility remains normal. Secondary amenorrhea is driven specifically by energy deficit (low EA < 30 kcal/kg FFM/day).
criteria: State that baseline physiological performance capacities (VO2max, strength, submaximal kinetics) remain stable across cycle phases.
Mention that elite performance and world records occur across all cycle phases.
Differentiate exercise stress vs energy deficit: energy deficit (low EA) drives amenorrhea, whereas high training volume with matched intake preserves LH pulsatility.

sa.prompt: Identify the three interrelated components of the Female Athlete Triad, and explain the cellular mechanism by which estrogen deficiency leads to accelerated bone mineral density loss and stress fractures.
sa.model: The Female Athlete Triad consists of three interrelated components along a clinical continuum: (1) Low Energy Availability (with or without disordered eating), (2) Menstrual Dysfunction (secondary amenorrhea), and (3) Low Bone Mineral Density (osteopenia/osteoporosis). Cellometrically, estrogen protects bone by stimulating osteoblast activity (bone formation) and suppressing osteoclast activity (bone resorption). In amenorrheic athletes, chronic hypoestrogenemia removes this protective brake on osteoclasts, causing bone resorption to exceed bone formation. Bone mineral density drops by 2% to 5% per year, eroding trabecular microarchitecture and markedly increasing the risk of cortical and trabecular stress fractures.
criteria: Identify all 3 components of the Triad (Low Energy Availability, Menstrual Dysfunction, Low Bone Mineral Density).

Three high-risk athletic categories are: (1) Appearance / Aesthetic sports (gymnastics, figure skating, ballet, diving); (2) Endurance sports (distance running, cross-country skiing); (3) Weight-classification sports (lightweight rowing, combat sports, horse racing jockeys).

Zero minutes (strict bed rest required)

60 minutes per month

mcq.q: Which maternal cardiorespiratory adaptation occurs during a healthy pregnancy?

Resting heart rate decreases to 20 beats/min
Cardiac output drops to zero during the second trimester

Bisk walking on level ground
Stationary cycling
Water aerobics in a cool pool

mcq.q: Why are contact sports (e.g., soccer, basketball, ice hockey) prohibited during pregnancy?

Risk of developing Type I diabetes within 5 minutes
Contact sports cause immediate bone loss in the fetus

mcq.q: What transient physiological response occurs during strenuous, maximal exercise exceeding 90% HRmax in pregnant elite athletes?

Immediate permanent cessation of fetal cardiac activity
Doubling of uterine artery diameter
Complete reversal of maternal blood circulation
mcq.rationale: Strenuous exercise exceeding 90% HRmax causes splanchnic vasoconstriction, evoking a transient 20% to 30% drop in uterine blood flow and transient fetal heart rate decelerations.

mcq.q: Which pregnancy-related metabolic complication is significantly reduced in incidence by regular maternal physical activity?

Type 1 juvenile diabetes
Sickle cell anemia
Hemophilia A
mcq.rationale: Regular exercise during pregnancy improves insulin sensitivity and glucose regulation, significantly reducing the risk of gestational diabetes.

mcq.q: Why should exercise in the supine position (lying flat on back) be avoided after the first trimester of pregnancy?

Supine position causes immediate uterine rupture
Supine position stops all fetal lung development
Supine position destroys maternal knee cartilage
mcq.rationale: After the first trimester, lying supine causes the enlarged uterus to compress the inferior vena cava, impairing venous return, lowering maternal cardiac output, and causing hypotension.

Increase in resting heart rate by 10 to 15 beats/min

sa.prompt: Summarize ACOG exercise guidelines during pregnancy (volume, intensity monitoring), list three maternal health benefits of regular exercise, and identify three prohibited activity types.
sa.model: ACOG guidelines recommend that pregnant women with uncomplicated pregnancies engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise per week (e.g., 30 minutes/day, 5 days/week). Exercise intensity should be monitored using Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE 12–14 on 6–20 scale) rather than target heart rate, as maternal heart rate kinetics are altered. Three key maternal health benefits include: (1) Reduced risk of gestational diabetes; (2) Decreased incidence of preeclampsia and hypertensive disorders; (3) Reduced excessive gestational weight gain and lower back pain. Three prohibited activity types are: (1) Scuba diving (risk of fetal decompression sickness); (2) Contact sports like soccer/basketball (risk of abdominal trauma/placental abruption); (3) High fall-risk sports like downhill skiing or horseback riding.

sa.prompt: Explain the cardiovascular changes that occur naturally during pregnancy, describe why supine exercise should be avoided after the first trimester, and discuss physiological considerations for elite pregnant athletes exercising at high intensity.
sa.model: During a normal pregnancy, maternal blood volume expands by 40% to 50%, resting heart rate increases by 10 to 15 bpm, and resting cardiac output increases by 30% to 50% to perfusion the placenta. Supine exercise should be avoided after the first trimester because the enlarged, heavy uterus compresses the inferior vena cava against the spine, drastically reducing venous return, stroke volume, and maternal cardiac output (causing supine hypotensive syndrome). For elite pregnant athletes engaging in high-intensity exercise (>90% HRmax), strenuous exertion induces transient splanchnic and uterine vasoconstriction, causing a temporary 20% to 30% reduction in uterine blood flow and transient fetal heart rate decelerations. High-intensity training requires careful hydration, cooling, and obstetric oversight.
criteria: Detail pregnancy cardiorespiratory changes (blood volume +40%-50%, resting HR +10-15 bpm, resting Q +30%-50%).
Explain supine avoidance (gravid uterus compresses inferior vena cava, impairing venous return and cardiac output).
